name: Jones calculus and the polarization coherency matrix
summary: Fully polarized light is a vector in C², and optical elements are 2×2 complex matrices that compose by multiplication. Partially polarized light is described by the Hermitian positive coherency matrix, which is mathematically a qubit density matrix, with the degree of polarization playing the role of purity. Birefringent principal axes are the eigenvectors of the symmetric dielectric tensor.
map: \mathbf E_{\rm out}=M_n\cdots M_1\mathbf E_{\rm in},\ J=\langle\mathbf E\mathbf E^\dagger\rangle,\ P=\sqrt{1-\frac{4\det J}{(\mathrm{tr}J)^2}}

name: Photonic bands as a Hermitian eigenvalue problem
summary: For lossless periodic dielectrics the master equation for H is a Hermitian eigenproblem, so frequencies are real, modes are orthogonal and a variational principle holds. Bloch's theorem then gives photonic bands and gaps, the same spectral theory as electrons in crystals. Unlike the electron case it acts on a transverse vector field with no intrinsic length scale, so scaling a crystal by s scales its frequencies by 1/s.
map: \nabla\times\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon(\mathbf r)}\nabla\times\mathbf H\right)=\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}\mathbf H,\quad \mathbf H_{\mathbf k}=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}\mathbf u_{\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)
sources: Yablonovitch (1987). "Inhibited Spontaneous Emission in Solid-State Physics and Electronics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2059. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2059)

name: The vector potential as a U(1) connection
summary: The gauge potential is a connection on a U(1) bundle and F is its curvature. Gauge transformations are changes of local section, and the Aharonov–Bohm phase is the connection's holonomy around a loop. A Dirac monopole is a topologically nontrivial bundle that needs two patches (Wu–Yang), and consistency between the patches quantizes charge.
map: A\to A+d\lambda,\ F=dA,\ e^{i(q/\hbar)\oint A}=e^{iq\Phi_B/\hbar},\ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{S^2}\frac{q}{\hbar}F\in\mathbb Z

name: Maxwell's equations as dF=0 and d⋆F=J
summary: In differential-form language the field strength is the exact 2-form F=dA. The homogeneous Maxwell equations are the Bianchi identity dF=0, and the sourced ones are d⋆F=⋆J. The integral laws are Stokes' theorem, the metric enters only through the Hodge star, and charge conservation follows from d²=0.

name: Transformation optics: geometry as an effective medium
summary: Maxwell's equations keep their form under any coordinate map if ε and μ are replaced by transformed tensors. A desired ray geometry, such as a cloak or a concentrator, is therefore designed as a coordinate transformation and built from anisotropic metamaterials. Equivalently, rays follow geodesics of an optical metric (Fermat's principle), the same mathematics that lets a medium mimic curved spacetime.
breaks: Ideal cloaks need singular, impedance-matched and strongly dispersive ε and μ, so causality and losses confine real devices to narrow bands or ray-only (carpet) versions.

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise and antenna temperature
summary: A matched single-mode antenna inside a blackbody enclosure delivers k_BTΔf to its load. That is exactly the available Johnson–Nyquist noise of a resistor at temperature T; Nyquist himself derived it from a transmission line in equilibrium. Radio astronomers therefore quote received power as an antenna or brightness temperature, with the radiation resistance acting as a resistor whose noise is the sky.
map: P=k_BT\,\Delta f,\ \langle V^2\rangle=4k_BTR\,\Delta f,\ T_A=\frac{1}{\Omega_A}\int T_B(\Omega)P_n(\Omega)\,d\Omega\ (h\nu\ll k_BT)

name: Super-resolution localization as parameter estimation
summary: PALM and STORM beat the diffraction limit through statistics rather than better optics. Isolated emitters are fitted by maximum likelihood, and the Cramér–Rao bound puts localization precision at about the PSF width divided by √N photons. Fisher-information analysis also shows that intensity imaging loses the ability to resolve two incoherent points as they merge ('Rayleigh's curse'), which mode-sorting measurements avoid.
sources: Betzig et al. (2006). "Imaging Intracellular Fluorescent Proteins at Nanometer Resolution". *Science* 313, 1642. [doi:10.1126/science.1127344](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1127344)

name: Faraday rotation (T-odd) vs optical activity (P-odd)
summary: Both effects rotate linear polarization. Natural optical activity comes from chirality (broken parity) and is reciprocal, so it undoes itself on retro-reflection. Faraday rotation is driven by the T-odd magnetic field and is nonreciprocal, so it doubles on the return pass. This symmetry difference is why optical isolators need magneto-optics.
map: \mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E+i\epsilon_0\mathbf G\times\mathbf E,\quad \mathbf G\propto\mathbf k\ (\text{activity, }\mathcal P\text{-odd})\ \text{or}\ \mathbf G\propto\mathbf B\ (\text{Faraday, }\mathcal T\text{-odd})

name: Inversion symmetry forbids second-order nonlinearity
summary: Under parity both P and E change sign, so every even-order susceptibility vanishes in a centrosymmetric medium. Second-harmonic generation therefore needs non-centrosymmetric crystals, such as the quartz in Franken's experiment or LiNbO₃. SHG is used as a probe of broken inversion at surfaces, at interfaces and in ferroelectric order.
map: P_i=\epsilon_0\chi^{(2)}_{ijk}E_jE_k;\ \mathcal P:\ \mathbf P\to-\mathbf P,\ \mathbf E\to-\mathbf E\Rightarrow\chi^{(2)}=-\chi^{(2)}=0
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)

name: T-breaking and absent Kramers protection for photons
summary: Photonic Chern insulators with one-way edge modes need broken time reversal, from gyromagnetic or time-modulated media. Photons are bosons with Θ²=+1, so they lack the Kramers degeneracy that protects electronic Z₂ topological insulators. Photonic 'quantum spin Hall' analogues instead use engineered pseudo-spins, which symmetry-breaking defects can couple.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)

name: Poincaré sphere: SU(2) on Jones vectors, SO(3) on Stokes
summary: Lossless polarization optics act on Jones vectors as SU(2), up to a global phase. The 2-to-1 homomorphism maps this to SO(3) rotations of the Stokes vector on the Poincaré sphere, the same structure as spin-½ on the Bloch sphere. A closed loop on the sphere gives the Pancharatnam geometric phase, equal to half the enclosed solid angle.
map: U=e^{-i\theta\,\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma/2}\mapsto R_{\hat{\mathbf n}}(\theta)\in SO(3),\ \mathbf S\propto\mathbf E^\dagger\boldsymbol\sigma\mathbf E,\ |\gamma_P|=\Omega/2

name: The field tensor as the (1,0)⊕(0,1) Lorentz representation
summary: Under the Lorentz group, F_{μν} splits into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts, the Riemann–Silberstein vectors E±icB, which transform as (1,0) and (0,1). Its two invariants are E²−c²B² and E·B. In Wigner's classification the photon is the massless helicity ±1 representation of the Poincaré group.
map:
\mathbf F_\pm=\mathbf E\pm ic\mathbf B\in(1,0),(0,1);\ F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}=2(B^2-E^2/c^2),\ F_{\mu
u}	ilde F^{\mu
u}\propto\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B
sources: Wigner (1939). "On Unitary Representations of the Inhomogeneous Lorentz Group". *Ann. Math.* 40, 149. [doi:10.2307/1968551](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968551)

name: Multipole moments as irreducible SO(3) tensors
summary: The 2l+1 spherical moments of order l form an irreducible representation of the rotation group, so a rank-l Cartesian moment reduces to its symmetric traceless part. The Wigner–Eckart theorem then gives the selection rules for multipole radiation. It also forbids moments of order l>2j in a state of angular momentum j, so a spin-½ particle has no quadrupole moment.

name: Spin and orbital angular momentum of light
summary: Rotational invariance gives the electromagnetic field a conserved angular momentum. For paraxial beams it splits into a spin part fixed by circular polarization (±ħ per photon, seen as torque on a wave plate by Beth in 1936) and an orbital part from helical phase fronts (ℓħ in Laguerre–Gauss beams). For general fields the split is gauge-sensitive and still debated.
map: \mathbf J=\epsilon_0\!\int\mathbf r\times(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)\,d^3r=\epsilon_0\!\int\big[E_i(\mathbf r\times\nabla)A_i+\mathbf E\times\mathbf A\big]d^3r\ (\text{Coulomb gauge})
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Conservation laws of electrodynamics as Noether currents
summary: The continuity equation is the Noether current of the U(1) phase symmetry of charged matter. Poynting's theorem and the Maxwell stress tensor are components of the field's (Belinfante-symmetrized) energy–momentum tensor, which comes from spacetime translations. By Noether's second theorem, local gauge invariance makes charge conservation an identity that Maxwell's equations themselves require.
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)
Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Phase matching as momentum conservation
summary: Translation invariance of a homogeneous crystal conserves photon momentum in wave mixing, so efficient conversion needs Δk=0, usually reached through birefringence. Quasi-phase-matching deliberately reduces continuous to discrete translation symmetry with periodic poling. Momentum is then conserved only up to the grating's reciprocal vector.

name: Plasma frequency as photon mass: Anderson's Higgs route
summary: In a collisionless Drude medium, transverse light obeys ω²=ω_p²+c²k², a massive Klein–Gordon dispersion. The long-range Coulomb force lifts the would-be acoustic density mode to the plasmon at ω_p. Anderson used this plasma picture to argue that a gauge field can gain mass by absorbing a would-be Goldstone mode, the core of the Higgs–Anderson mechanism.
breaks: A normal plasma has no condensate and no broken symmetry. A collisionless plasma only freezes in static magnetic flux, like a perfect conductor, while a superconductor expels it (Meissner effect) because its photon mass comes from a phase-coherent condensate. With collisions, static fields penetrate fully.

name: Laser threshold as spontaneous U(1) phase breaking
summary: Near threshold the single-mode field amplitude obeys a Landau-like equation. Below threshold only zero field is stable; above it there is a ring of states with fixed amplitude and arbitrary phase. The phase is then a Goldstone-like soft mode, and its diffusion under spontaneous-emission noise sets the Schawlow–Townes linewidth.
breaks: A laser is an open, driven-dissipative system rather than an equilibrium ground state. A single mode is effectively zero-dimensional, so the phase diffuses freely (finite linewidth). There is no true long-range order or thermodynamic singularity, only a crossover that sharpens with photon number.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Rayleigh's λ⁻⁴ law from dimensional analysis
summary: Rayleigh (1871) argued that for a particle much smaller than the wavelength, the scattered amplitude is proportional to its volume and falls off as 1/r. Dimensional consistency then forces a 1/λ² factor in amplitude, hence λ⁻⁴ in intensity, which is why the sky is blue. It is the textbook example of a scaling argument.
breaks: It holds only for size parameter 2πa/λ≪1 and away from resonances. For a≳λ the full Mie solution, with its resonances and nearly wavelength-independent scattering, takes over (white clouds).
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)
Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

name: Mode-locked frequency combs as rulers for constants
summary: A mode-locked laser emits a comb of evenly spaced frequencies, and f–2f self-referencing fixes its offset. This links optical frequencies to the caesium microwave standard, enabling hydrogen spectroscopy for the Rydberg constant and optical-clock limits on drifts of α. Earlier laser frequency and wavelength measurements had already led to fixing c exactly in 1983.
sources: Tiesinga et al. (2021). "CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants: 2018". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 93, 025010. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010)

name: Ampere redefinition: μ0 became a measured constant
summary: Until 2019 the ampere was defined by the magnetostatic force between parallel wires, which fixed μ0=4π×10⁻⁷ N A⁻² exactly. Fixing e and h instead makes μ0 a measured quantity tied to the fine-structure constant. CODATA 2022 gives μ0=1.256 637 061 27(20)×10⁻⁶ N A⁻², within 1σ of the old exact value.
sources: Stock et al. (2019). "The revision of the SI—the result of three decades of progress in metrology". *Metrologia* 56, 022001. [doi:10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013](https://doi.org/10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013)

name: Spin-glass methods for learning and inference
summary: Replica, cavity and message-passing methods built for spin glasses and random constraint satisfaction became tools for analysing and designing learning and inference algorithms, such as belief and survey propagation and loss-landscape studies. In the other direction, ML is now used to detect order in disordered systems.
sources: Mézard, Parisi & Zecchina (2002). "Analytic and Algorithmic Solution of Random Satisfiability Problems". *Science* 297, 812. [doi:10.1126/science.1073287](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1073287)

name: Learning machines as statistical-mechanical systems
summary: Neural networks are both a tool for physics (surrogates, neural quantum states) and an object studied by statistical mechanics. Hopfield nets and Boltzmann machines are Ising-type energy models, and their capacity and generalization are computed with replica and cavity methods.
map: E(\mathbf s)=-\tfrac12\sum_{ij}J_{ij}s_is_j,\quad P(\mathbf s)\propto e^{-E(\mathbf s)/T}
sources: Hopfield (1982). "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities". *PNAS* 79, 2554. [doi:10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.79.8.2554)
Carleo et al. (2019). "Machine learning and the physical sciences". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 045002. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.91.045002](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.91.045002)

name: Diffusion models: Langevin dynamics run backwards
summary: Diffusion generative models add noise with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (forward Fokker–Planck) process. They generate samples by integrating the time-reversed SDE, whose drift contains the learned score $\nabla\log p_t$, a construction taken from non-equilibrium statistical physics.
sources: Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015). "Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics". *ICML*. [arXiv:1503.03585](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03585)
Song et al. (2021). "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations". *ICLR*. [arXiv:2011.13456](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456)

name: Deep networks as renormalization (analogy)
summary: Mehta and Schwab mapped stacked restricted Boltzmann machines onto Kadanoff block-spin variational RG, which suggests that network depth performs coarse-graining. Later information-theoretic schemes used neural networks to learn the relevant RG variables directly.
breaks: The mapping is exact only for one particular variational RG. Trained networks need not follow an RG flow and impose no scale invariance or fixed-point structure, and supervised nets discard information for reasons unrelated to scale.
sources: Mehta & Schwab (2014). "An exact mapping between the Variational Renormalization Group and Deep Learning". [arXiv:1410.3831](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3831)
Koch-Janusz & Ringel (2018). "Mutual information, neural networks and the renormalization group". *Nature Physics* 14, 578. [doi:10.1038/s41567-018-0081-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-018-0081-4)

name: Thermostats and ergodic averages realise ensembles
summary: Plain MD samples the microcanonical ensemble through time averages along an ergodic trajectory. Nosé–Hoover extended dynamics and Langevin thermostats are built so that the physical variables are canonically distributed, and barostats give NPT.
sources: Nosé (1984). "A unified formulation of the constant temperature molecular dynamics methods". *J. Chem. Phys.* 81, 511. [doi:10.1063/1.447334](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.447334)
Hoover (1985). "Canonical dynamics: Equilibrium phase-space distributions". *Phys. Rev. A* 31, 1695. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.31.1695](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.31.1695)

name: MD discovers long-time tails beyond Boltzmann
summary: Alder and Wainwright's MD showed that a fluid's velocity autocorrelation decays as a power law, not exponentially as the Boltzmann equation's molecular-chaos assumption predicts. The cause is correlated vortex backflow, which also makes Green–Kubo transport coefficients diverge in 2D.
sources: Alder & Wainwright (1970). "Decay of the Velocity Autocorrelation Function". *Phys. Rev. A* 1, 18. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.1.18](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.1.18)

name: Fortuin–Kasteleyn clusters behind Swendsen–Wang
summary: The q-state Potts partition function equals a random-cluster model that reduces to bond percolation at q=1. Swendsen–Wang and Wolff algorithms flip exactly these FK clusters, so the Ising transition is a percolation transition of FK clusters.
sources: Fortuin & Kasteleyn (1972). "On the random-cluster model: I. Introduction and relation to other models". *Physica* 57, 536. [doi:10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-8914(72)90045-6)
Swendsen & Wang (1987). "Nonuniversal critical dynamics in Monte Carlo simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 86. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.86)

name: Parallel tempering and simulated annealing
summary: Rugged spin-glass landscapes trap local Monte Carlo, which led to replica-exchange (parallel tempering) swaps between temperatures. The transfer also ran the other way: simulated annealing turned the slow cooling of a frustrated system into a general optimization algorithm.
sources: Hukushima & Nemoto (1996). "Exchange Monte Carlo Method and Application to Spin Glass Simulations". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 65, 1604. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.65.1604](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.65.1604)
Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983). "Optimization by Simulated Annealing". *Science* 220, 671. [doi:10.1126/science.220.4598.671](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.220.4598.671)

name: Path-integral Monte Carlo of Bose and Fermi statistics
summary: Imaginary-time path integrals turn quantum particles into classical ring polymers. Bose statistics enter as permutation cycles whose winding gives the superfluid fraction of He-4 at the λ point, while Fermi antisymmetry produces negative weights: the sign problem.
sources: Ceperley (1995). "Path integrals in the theory of condensed helium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 67, 279. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.67.279](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.67.279)

Troyer & Wiese (2005). "Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 94, 170201. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.94.170201](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.94.170201)

name: MCMC is a master equation with detailed balance
summary: A Metropolis or Glauber chain is a discrete-time master equation whose stationary state is the Boltzmann weight, and its relaxation is a genuine stochastic (model-A) dynamics. Langevin and hybrid Monte Carlo sample by integrating Langevin or Hamiltonian dynamics.
sources: Hastings (1970). "Monte Carlo sampling methods using Markov chains and their applications". *Biometrika* 57, 97. [doi:10.1093/biomet/57.1.97](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/57.1.97)

name: Annealed importance sampling equals Jarzynski equality
summary: Averaging exponentiated work over non-equilibrium switching runs to estimate a free-energy difference is Jarzynski's equality. Statistics independently introduced the same estimator as annealed importance sampling, and in both the variance is controlled by the dissipated work.
sources: Jarzynski (1997). "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 78, 2690. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690)
Neal (2001). "Annealed importance sampling". *Statistics and Computing* 11, 125. [doi:10.1023/A:1008923215028](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008923215028)

name: Finite-size scaling extraction of critical exponents
summary: Monte Carlo gets precise critical exponents from finite-size scaling: Binder-cumulant crossings locate $T_c$, and histogram reweighting maps observables continuously in $T$. Monte Carlo values for 3D Ising now agree with the conformal bootstrap to about four significant figures.
sources: Ferrenberg & Swendsen (1988). "New Monte Carlo technique for studying phase transitions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 61, 2635. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2635](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.61.2635)
Binder (1981). "Finite size scaling analysis of Ising model block distribution functions". *Z. Phys. B* 43, 119. [doi:10.1007/BF01293604](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01293604)

name: Metropolis and cluster sampling of lattice models
summary: Markov-chain Monte Carlo that obeys detailed balance with respect to $e^{-\beta H}$ is the standard numerical route to Ising, Potts, XY and Heisenberg thermodynamics. Swendsen–Wang and Wolff cluster moves remove the critical slowing down that local updates suffer.
map: P_{\rm acc}=\min(1,e^{-\beta\Delta E}),\quad \tau\sim\xi^{z},\ z_{\rm local}\approx2,\ z_{\rm cluster}\ll2
sources: Metropolis et al. (1953). "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines". *J. Chem. Phys.* 21, 1087. [doi:10.1063/1.1699114](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114)
Wolff (1989). "Collective Monte Carlo Updating for Spin Systems". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 62, 361. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.62.361](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.62.361)

name: Lattice Boltzmann: kinetic theory as fluid solver
summary: Discretizing the Boltzmann equation with a BGK collision term on a velocity lattice gives a local, highly parallel CFD scheme. A Chapman–Enskog expansion shows that it reproduces Navier–Stokes, with the viscosity set by the relaxation time.
map: f_i(\mathbf x+\mathbf c_i\Delta t,t+\Delta t)-f_i=-\tfrac1\tau(f_i-f_i^{\rm eq}),\quad \nu=c_s^2(\tau-\tfrac12)\Delta t
sources: Chen & Doolen (1998). "Lattice Boltzmann method for fluid flows". *Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech.* 30, 329. [doi:10.1146/annurev.fluid.30.1.329](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.fluid.30.1.329)

name: DMRG and tensor RG as renormalization
summary: DMRG grew out of Wilson's numerical RG by keeping the most heavily weighted density-matrix eigenstates. Tensor RG, Baxter-style corner transfer matrices and MERA coarse-grain classical partition functions and quantum states, carrying out real-space RG flows with controlled truncation and giving scaling dimensions at fixed points.
sources: White (1992). "Density matrix formulation for quantum renormalization groups". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 69, 2863. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863)

Levin & Nave (2007). "Tensor Renormalization Group Approach to Two-Dimensional Classical Lattice Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 99, 120601. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.120601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.120601)

name: Blackbody and heat capacities launched quantum theory
summary: Planck's 1900 fit to blackbody radiation required energy quanta $h\nu$ and gave the first accurate $k_B$ and $N_A$. Einstein's 1907 quantized-oscillator heat capacity then explained the low-T failure of Dulong–Petit, and Bose's 1924 counting led to Bose–Einstein statistics.

name: Brownian motion proved atoms real
summary: Einstein's 1905 theory tied the diffusion constant of a suspended particle to $k_BT$ and viscosity, and Perrin's 1908–09 measurements of it gave Avogadro's number and settled the atomic debate. Langevin's 1908 equation founded the theory of stochastic differential equations.

name: Arrow of time and the second law
summary: The second law is philosophy's central example of an irreversible macroscopic law resting on time-symmetric microdynamics. The standard reductive account combines $S=k_B\ln W$ with a low-entropy initial condition (the past hypothesis), and the status of that account is still debated.

name: Maxwell's demon and Landauer: is information physical?
summary: In the Bennett–Landauer account, Maxwell's demon is defeated by the $k_BT\ln2$ cost of erasing its memory. Philosophers such as Earman and Norton dispute whether Landauer's principle is independently established, even though experiments have confirmed the erasure bound.
sources: Landauer (1961). "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process". *IBM J. Res. Dev.* 5, 183. [doi:10.1147/rd.53.0183](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: H-theorem and the Loschmidt–Zermelo objections
summary: Boltzmann's H-theorem derives a monotonic entropy increase from the Boltzmann equation. Loschmidt's reversal objection and Zermelo's recurrence objection traced the time asymmetry to the molecular-chaos assumption (Stosszahlansatz), now the standard case study of irreversibility emerging from reversible laws.

name: Universality, emergence and the thermodynamic limit
summary: Phase transitions are non-analyticities that exist only in the $N\to\infty$ limit, and universality makes critical exponents independent of microscopic detail. Both are the main case studies in the reduction-versus-emergence and multiple-realizability debates, from Anderson's 'More is different' to Batterman.
sources: Anderson (1972). "More Is Different". *Science* 177, 393. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4047.393](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393)

name: Kramers–Kronig relations from causality
summary: Causality makes the response function $\chi(\omega)$ analytic in the upper half-plane. Contour integration then gives the Kramers–Kronig relations between its reactive and dissipative parts, plus sum rules, and analytic continuation from Matsubara frequencies gives real-time response.
sources: Toll (1956). "Causality and the Dispersion Relation: Logical Foundations". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 1760. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.1760](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.1760)

Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I. General Theory and Simple Applications to Magnetic and Conduction Problems". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Lee–Yang zeros: transitions as complex zeros of Z
summary: For finite N the partition function is a polynomial in the fugacity with no positive real zeros. The Lee–Yang circle theorem places every zero of the ferromagnetic Ising model on $|z|=1$, and a transition appears where the zeros pinch the real axis as $N\to\infty$; Fisher zeros do the same in complex β.
sources: Lee & Yang (1952). "Statistical Theory of Equations of State and Phase Transitions. II. Lattice Gas and Ising Model". *Phys. Rev.* 87, 410. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.87.410](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410)

name: Response functions are retarded Green's functions
summary: The Kubo formula writes the susceptibility as a retarded commutator Green's function, so linear response is a Green's-function convolution with the force. Causality enters through $\theta(t)$, and the poles give the normal modes and their damping.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I. General Theory and Simple Applications to Magnetic and Conduction Problems". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Fokker–Planck propagators as Green's functions
summary: The transition probability of Brownian motion is the Green's function (heat kernel) of the diffusion or Fokker–Planck operator. First-passage and escape problems are solved with images, Laplace transforms and Sturm–Liouville eigenmodes, and the symmetrized Fokker–Planck operator maps onto a Schrödinger operator.
sources: Chandrasekhar (1943). "Stochastic Problems in Physics and Astronomy". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 15, 1. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1)

Kramers (1940). "Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)

name: Transfer-matrix eigenvalues give the free energy
summary: With local couplings, $Z=\mathrm{Tr}\,T^N$, so the free energy comes from the largest transfer-matrix eigenvalue and the correlation length from the ratio of the top two. Perron–Frobenius makes the top eigenvalue unique, which rules out a 1D transition at T>0, and Onsager solved 2D Ising by diagonalizing its transfer matrix.
sources: Kramers & Wannier (1941). "Statistics of the Two-Dimensional Ferromagnet. Part I". *Phys. Rev.* 60, 252. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.60.252](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.60.252)
Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

name: Carathéodory: second law as integrability of δQ
summary: In Carathéodory's formulation, heat is an inexact Pfaffian 1-form. The axiom that every state has adiabatically inaccessible neighbours implies the form is integrable, and its integrating factor yields absolute temperature and entropy from differential geometry alone.
sources: Lieb & Yngvason (1999). "The physics and mathematics of the second law of thermodynamics". *Phys. Rep.* 310, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00082-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00082-9)

name: Canonical energy fluctuations limit microcalorimeters
summary: A microcalorimeter or bolometer weakly linked to a bath has canonical energy fluctuations $\langle\Delta E^2\rangle=k_BT^2C$. This thermodynamic-fluctuation noise sets the ultimate resolution of transition-edge sensors, which is why they operate near 0.1 K with tiny heat capacity.
sources: Irwin (1995). "An application of electrothermal feedback for high resolution cryogenic particle detection". *Appl. Phys. Lett.* 66, 1998. [doi:10.1063/1.113674](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.113674)

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise as fluctuation–dissipation
summary: The thermal noise floor $4k_BTR\Delta f$ of every resistor and amplifier is the fluctuation–dissipation theorem applied to a circuit. The theorem's quantum form adds the zero-point term behind the half-photon-per-mode limit of linear amplifiers.
sources: Nyquist (1928). "Thermal Agitation of Electric Charge in Conductors". *Phys. Rev.* 32, 110. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.32.110](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.32.110)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Phase transitions in high-dimensional inference
summary: Planted (teacher–student) problems such as community detection, compressed sensing and perceptron learning are disordered systems, and replica or cavity calculations give their Bayes-optimal error. They show sharp detectability and algorithmic-hardness thresholds, and Bayes-optimal inference sits on the Nishimori line, where replica symmetry holds.
sources: Zdeborová & Krzakala (2016). "Statistical physics of inference: thresholds and algorithms". *Adv. Phys.* 65, 453. [doi:10.1080/00018732.2016.1211393](https://doi.org/10.1080/00018732.2016.1211393)
Gardner (1988). "The space of interactions in neural network models". *J. Phys. A* 21, 257. [doi:10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030)

name: Maximum entropy: statistical mechanics as inference
summary: Jaynes showed that the Gibbs ensembles are the maximum-Shannon-entropy distributions consistent with measured averages, so inference and statistical mechanics share the exponential family. In Bayesian terms the evidence plays the role of a partition function and $-\ln$(evidence) that of a free energy.
map: \max_p\Big[-\sum p\ln p\Big]\ \text{s.t.}\ \langle E\rangle\ \Rightarrow\ p\propto e^{-\beta E}
sources: Jaynes (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev.* 106, 620. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.106.620](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620)
Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)

name: Cramér–Rao bound and thermodynamic uncertainty
summary: The thermodynamic uncertainty relation bounds the relative precision of any current by the entropy produced. It follows from the Cramér–Rao inequality applied to a perturbed path ensemble, so dissipation plays the role of the Fisher information that limits precision.
sources: Barato & Seifert (2015). "Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation for Biomolecular Processes". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 114, 158101. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.158101](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.158101)

Hasegawa & Van Vu (2019). "Uncertainty relations in stochastic processes: An information inequality approach". *Phys. Rev. E* 99, 062126. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.99.062126](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.99.062126)

name: Variational Bayes is mean-field theory
summary: Fitting a factorized approximate posterior by maximizing the evidence lower bound is the Gibbs–Bogoliubov–Feynman variational principle of naive mean-field theory. Belief propagation corresponds to the Bethe approximation, and the TAP equations add the Onsager reaction term.
map: F\le F_0+\langle H-H_0\rangle_0\ \Leftrightarrow\ \ln p(D)\ge\mathbb E_q[\ln p(D,\theta)]-\mathbb E_q[\ln q]
sources: Yedidia, Freeman & Weiss (2005). "Constructing free-energy approximations and generalized belief propagation algorithms". *IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory* 51, 2282. [doi:10.1109/TIT.2005.850085](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2005.850085)

name: Permutation symmetry gives Bose and Fermi statistics
summary: Identical particles carry a one-dimensional representation of the permutation group $S_N$: symmetric for bosons, antisymmetric for fermions. These give Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac occupation numbers, and in 2D the braid group also allows anyons.

name: Symmetry classifies phases and transitions
summary: Phases differ by which subgroup $H\subset G$ of the symmetry group the state keeps, and the order parameter transforms in a representation of $G$. Together with the dimension, $G$ and $H$ fix the allowed Landau free energy, the order-parameter manifold $G/H$ and its defects, and the universality class.

name: Onsager reciprocity from time-reversal invariance
summary: Time-reversal symmetry of the microscopic dynamics implies the Onsager–Casimir relations among transport coefficients, such as the Kelvin relation between the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients. The relations carry sign factors for T-odd variables and require reversing magnetic fields.
sources: Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)

name: Virasoro symmetry solves 2D critical models
summary: At 2D critical points, scale invariance grows into the infinite-dimensional Virasoro algebra. Its unitary minimal-model representations give exact exponents, e.g. Ising with $c=1/2$, $\eta=1/4$, $\nu=1$, which match Onsager's lattice solution.
sources: Belavin, Polyakov & Zamolodchikov (1984). "Infinite conformal symmetry in two-dimensional quantum field theory". *Nucl. Phys. B* 241, 333. [doi:10.1016/0550-3213(84)90052-X](https://doi.org/10.1016/0550-3213(84)90052-X)

name: Order-parameter symmetry labels universality classes
summary: A universality class is fixed by the dimension and the order parameter's symmetry group: Z2 (Ising), O(2) (XY, He-4), O(3) (Heisenberg) or S_q (Potts). The representation content of a perturbation, such as cubic anisotropy, decides whether it is relevant.
sources: Pelissetto & Vicari (2002). "Critical phenomena and renormalization-group theory". *Phys. Rep.* 368, 549. [doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3)

name: Conserved charges fix the Gibbs ensemble
summary: Each Noether charge (energy, U(1) particle number, momentum) enters the equilibrium ensemble with its own Lagrange multiplier ($\beta$, $\beta\mu$, $\beta\mathbf v$). Integrable systems, which have extensively many conserved quantities, relax instead to a generalized Gibbs ensemble.
sources: Rigol et al. (2007). "Relaxation in a Completely Integrable Many-Body Quantum System: An Ab Initio Study of the Dynamics of the Highly Excited States of 1D Lattice Hard-Core Bosons". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 98, 050405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.050405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.050405)

name: Replica symmetry breaking vs. ordinary SSB
summary: Parisi's solution of the SK model breaks the permutation symmetry among $n\to0$ replicas. The Edwards–Anderson overlap then acts as an order parameter for frozen random order, as ergodicity splits into many pure states.
breaks: No symmetry of the physical Hamiltonian breaks: replica symmetry exists only inside the $n\to0$ formalism, and the pure states are not related by any group action. Whether finite-dimensional spin glasses follow RSB or the droplet picture is still disputed.
sources: Sherrington & Kirkpatrick (1975). "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 35, 1792. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

name: BEC as broken U(1); Goldstone modes set low-T laws
summary: Bose–Einstein condensation is off-diagonal long-range order, a broken global U(1) phase whose Goldstone mode is the Bogoliubov phonon. More generally, Goldstone dispersion sets low-T power laws: linear phonons give Debye $C\propto T^3$, and quadratic ferromagnetic magnons give Bloch $\Delta M\propto T^{3/2}$.
sources: Penrose & Onsager (1956). "Bose-Einstein Condensation and Liquid Helium". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 576. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.576](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.576)

name: Landau free energy is the symmetry-breaking potential
summary: The Landau expansion and the Mexican-hat (Higgs) potential are the same symmetric quartic, and its minimum moves off the origin when the quadratic coefficient changes sign. Mean-field theory then gives $m\propto(T_c-T)^{1/2}$, and the Ginzburg criterion says when fluctuations invalidate it.
breaks: Landau theory is a thermal free energy with a T-dependent coefficient, valid above the upper critical dimension. When the symmetry is gauged there is no local gauge-invariant order parameter (Elitzur's theorem) and the Goldstone modes are absorbed by the gauge field.

name: Mermin–Wagner and quasi-long-range order
summary: In 2D, Goldstone fluctuations forbid continuous symmetry breaking at T>0 (Mermin–Wagner), but the XY model still has a transition. Vortices, classified by $\pi_1(U(1))=\mathbb Z$, unbind at $T_{\rm BKT}$ and separate power-law from exponential correlations.
sources: Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)

Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)

name: Anomalous dimensions: where naive scaling fails
summary: Dimensional analysis and generalized homogeneity (Widom scaling) predict power laws, but near criticality the microscopic cutoff never drops out, so exponents pick up anomalous dimensions; Barenblatt calls this incomplete similarity. The RG computes them as eigenvalues at a fixed point.
sources: Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)
Widom (1965). "Equation of State in the Neighborhood of the Critical Point". *J. Chem. Phys.* 43, 3898. [doi:10.1063/1.1696618](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1696618)

name: Kelvin redefined by fixing the Boltzmann constant
summary: Thermodynamic temperature, defined through the second law by Kelvin's Carnot scale, has been realized since 2019 by fixing $k_B$ exactly. The fixed value came from primary thermometry based on statistical mechanics: acoustic gas thermometry ($u^2=\gamma k_BT/m$), dielectric-constant gas thermometry and Johnson-noise thermometry.

name: Neural quantum states and volume-law entanglement
summary: Neural networks such as restricted Boltzmann machines and transformers serve as variational wavefunctions trained by variational Monte Carlo. An MPS's entanglement is capped at ln χ, but these networks can encode volume-law entanglement with polynomially many parameters (Deng, Li & Das Sarma 2017).

name: Born–Oppenheimer surfaces drive ab initio MD
summary: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation separates electrons from nuclei, with small parameter (m_e/M)^{1/4}. Ab initio and Car–Parrinello MD move classical nuclei on the electronic ground-state energy surface. The approximation fails at conical intersections, where nonadiabatic methods such as surface hopping take over.

name: Amplitude estimation speeds up Monte Carlo quadratically
summary: Amplitude amplification estimates an expectation value to error ε with O(1/ε) oracle calls, against O(1/ε²) samples classically (Montanaro 2015). It is the same 1/√N to 1/N jump as from the standard quantum limit to the Heisenberg limit.

name: Path-integral quantum Monte Carlo and the sign problem
summary: Slicing imaginary time turns the quantum partition function into a classical ensemble of ring polymers that Metropolis sampling can handle. This is exact for bosons, but fermion exchange produces negative weights. That is the sign problem, which is NP-hard in general (Troyer–Wiese 2005).

name: Trotter splitting: symplectic integrators and quantum gates
summary: Leapfrog and Strang symplectic integrators and split-step Schrödinger solvers use the same operator splitting that compiles e^{-iHt} into gates on a quantum computer. Higher-order Suzuki formulas and their commutator error bounds carry over directly.

name: Area-law entanglement makes MPS and DMRG efficient
summary: The Schmidt rank across any cut of a matrix product state is at most the bond dimension, so the entanglement entropy obeys S ≤ ln χ. Ground states of gapped 1D Hamiltonians obey an area law (Hastings 2007), so they compress efficiently, and entanglement growth sets the cost of time evolution.

name: Tensor-network contraction vs quantum-advantage claims
summary: After the random-circuit-sampling advantage claims (Arute et al. 2019), tensor-network contraction simulated the same circuits classically far faster than first estimated. The treewidth of a circuit's tensor network sets the classical cost, so tensor networks mark the moving boundary of quantum advantage.

name: Bohr–Einstein debates and the EPR argument
summary: The 1927–35 Bohr–Einstein debates and the EPR argument treated completeness and locality as philosophical questions. Bell (1964) turned them into testable inequalities, which is why foundations of QM is where history and philosophy meet the laboratory.

name: The quantum revolution, 1900–1927
summary: Blackbody radiation (Planck 1900), the photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905) and atomic spectra with the Bohr model (1913) led to matrix and wave mechanics (1925–26). Spectroscopy drove the experiments, and the episode is the standard case study of theory change.

name: No-go theorems as experimental metaphysics
summary: The Bell, Kochen–Specker and PBR theorems turn questions about hidden variables, locality and the reality of the wavefunction into constraints that experiments can test. Philosophy of physics now argues over which premise to give up, such as measurement independence or outcome independence.

name: Measurement problem and rival interpretations
summary: Unitary evolution and definite measurement outcomes conflict. Copenhagen, Everett's relative states, Bohmian mechanics, GRW collapse and QBism resolve this in different ways, and the meaning of Born-rule probability in many worlds is debated in both fields.

name: Typicality and ETH as foundations of statistical mechanics
summary: Philosophy of statistical mechanics asks why equilibrium ensembles work. Canonical typicality (almost every pure state of system plus bath has a thermal reduced state) and ETH (every energy eigenstate looks thermal) answer this for isolated quantum systems without ensembles or the ergodic hypothesis.

name: Eigenproblems and special functions of quantum mechanics
summary: Separation of variables, Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems and orthogonal polynomials (Hermite, Laguerre, Legendre) give the textbook spectra. Green's functions, contour integrals and asymptotic methods underpin perturbation theory, scattering and WKB.

name: Saddle points, Stokes lines and instantons
summary: Semiclassics evaluates the path integral by stationary phase or steepest descent. Airy functions join WKB solutions at turning points, Stokes phenomena control tunnelling exponents, and Wick rotation turns tunnelling into Euclidean instanton saddles.
map: \int\mathcal Dx\,e^{iS/\hbar}\approx\sum_{\rm cl}A_{\rm cl}\,e^{iS_{\rm cl}/\hbar},\ t\to-i\tau,\ \Gamma\propto e^{-S_E^{\rm inst}/\hbar}

name: Analytic S-matrix: poles, resonances, dispersion
summary: Causality makes partial-wave S-matrices analytic in complex momentum. Bound states are poles on the positive imaginary k axis and resonances are poles below the real axis that give Breit–Wigner peaks. The optical theorem and dispersion relations tie forward amplitudes to total cross sections.

name: Lippmann–Schwinger equation and the Born series
summary: The outgoing Helmholtz Green's function turns the Schrödinger equation into an integral equation. Iterating it gives the Born series, and its far-field limit gives the scattering amplitude f(θ).
map: \psi=\phi+G_0^{(+)}V\psi,\ G_0^{(+)}(\mathbf r,\mathbf r')=-\frac{m}{2\pi\hbar^2}\frac{e^{ik|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Schmidt decomposition is the singular value decomposition
summary: Arrange a bipartite pure state's amplitudes as a matrix and its SVD is the Schmidt form. The squared singular values are the eigenvalues of the reduced state, so entanglement entropy and Schmidt rank are matrix invariants. The same SVD truncation drives DMRG.

name: Dirac notation and operator algebra
summary: The working tools of QM are linear-algebra results: commutators and simultaneous diagonalisation, unitary changes of basis, ladder-operator algebras, and rigged Hilbert spaces for the continuous spectra of position and momentum.

name: Spectral theorem as the measurement postulate
summary: States are rays in a Hilbert space and observables are self-adjoint operators. The spectral theorem supplies the possible outcomes (eigenvalues) and projectors that give the Born rule and state update. Gleason's theorem shows this is the only consistent probability measure for dimension ≥ 3.

name: Berry phase as holonomy of a U(1) connection
summary: The Berry connection is a connection on the line bundle of eigenstates over parameter space. Its curvature 2-form integrates to the Berry phase, and over closed surfaces to integer Chern numbers (Simon 1983). The quantum geometric tensor combines the Fubini–Study metric with the Berry curvature.
sources: Berry (1984). "Quantal phase factors accompanying adiabatic changes". *Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A* 392, 45. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1984.0023](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1984.0023)

name: Quantum-limited amplifiers for qubit readout
summary: Dispersive readout of superconducting qubits needs Josephson parametric or travelling-wave amplifiers that work near the Caves bound: a phase-insensitive amplifier must add at least half a quantum of noise. The same SQUID and Josephson technology reads out cryogenic detectors.

name: Cryogenic sensors as single-photon detectors
summary: Cryogenic sensors and the noise analysis of instrumentation have become quantum-optics hardware. Transition-edge sensors resolve photon number with about 95% efficiency, and superconducting nanowire detectors reach about 98% efficiency with few-picosecond jitter. Dark counts and dead time are the other figures of merit.

name: Quantum Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
summary: Optimising the classical Cramér–Rao bound over all quantum measurements gives the quantum Fisher information (Braunstein–Caves 1994). N independent probes give F_Q = N, the standard quantum limit; entangled probes reach up to N², the Heisenberg limit.

name: Clock uncertainty budgets and Allan deviation
summary: Clock accuracy is quoted as a GUM-style budget of Type B systematic shifts (blackbody, Zeeman, Stark, motional) added in quadrature. Stability is quoted as the Allan deviation, which quantum projection noise ultimately limits. This is how the Al+/Hg+ ratio reached the 17th decimal place.
sources: Rosenband et al. (2008). "Frequency Ratio of Al+and Hg+Single-Ion Optical Clocks; Metrology at the 17th Decimal Place". *Science* 319, 1808. [doi:10.1126/science.1154622](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1154622)

name: Rotation symmetry labels states and selection rules
summary: Rotational invariance of H makes j and m good quantum numbers. The Wigner–Eckart theorem splits every tensor-operator matrix element into a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient times a reduced element, which gives the dipole selection rules.

name: Atomic parity violation and electron EDM searches
summary: Z-boson exchange mixes S and P states, so the forbidden Cs 6S–7S transition gains a parity-odd amplitude that measures the weak charge Q_W (Wood et al. 1997). Electron-EDM searches in heavy atoms and polar molecules test T, and hence CP, violation; the best bound is |d_e| < 4.1×10^{-30} e·cm (JILA HfF+, 2023).

name: PT symmetry and exceptional points
summary: A non-Hermitian Hamiltonian that commutes with the antiunitary PT operator has a real spectrum while the symmetry is unbroken. At the breaking threshold, eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce at an exceptional point: H becomes a non-diagonalisable Jordan block, the eigenvalues meet at a square-root branch point, and the splitting grows as √ε.
sources: Bender & Boettcher (1998). "Real Spectra in Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians Having P T Symmetry". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 80, 5243. [doi:10.1103/physrevlett.80.5243](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.80.5243)

name: Dyson's threefold way fixes chaotic level statistics
summary: Spectra of chaotic systems follow random-matrix statistics (Bohigas–Giannoni–Schmit 1984). Antiunitary symmetry picks the ensemble: GOE if T² = +1, GUE if T is broken, GSE if T² = −1. The level-repulsion exponent β is the diagnostic.

name: Kramers degeneracy from T² = −1 for half-integer spin
summary: Time reversal is antiunitary and acts on spin as Θ = e^{-iπS_y/ħ}K, so Θ² = (−1)^{2S}. With an odd number of electrons, every level is at least doubly degenerate unless a magnetic field breaks T. This is the origin of the protected Kramers pairs in topological insulators.

name: Spin is a projective representation of SO(3)
summary: Angular-momentum operators obey the su(2) algebra, whose irreducible representations give j = 0, 1/2, 1, …. Half-integer spin exists because SU(2) double-covers SO(3): a 2π rotation multiplies a spinor by −1, as seen in neutron interferometry.

name: Hidden SO(4) symmetry of the hydrogen atom
summary: On bound states, the angular momentum L and the scaled Runge–Lenz vector K generate so(4) ≅ su(2)⊕su(2). Pauli (1926) used this to obtain the Bohr levels algebraically, and it explains the n² degeneracy across ℓ. SU(3) plays the same role for the 3D isotropic oscillator.

name: Quantum Noether: conserved generators commute with H
summary: By Wigner's theorem, symmetries act as unitary or antiunitary operators. If a continuous symmetry e^{-iθG/ħ} leaves H invariant, then [G,H] = 0 and the distribution of G is conserved. This is the operator form of Noether's theorem: momentum from translations, J from rotations, charge from U(1).

name: BEC breaks U(1); Bogoliubov phonon is the Goldstone mode
summary: The condensate order parameter ψ = √n e^{iθ} breaks the global phase symmetry that goes with atom-number conservation. The gapless Bogoliubov sound mode is the Goldstone boson, and its sound speed sets the Landau critical velocity for superfluid flow.

name: Time crystals break time-translation symmetry
summary: Wilczek's (2012) equilibrium time crystal is ruled out by the Watanabe–Oshikawa no-go theorem. Instead, periodically driven many-body systems, which conserve quasienergy rather than energy, break the discrete Floquet time-translation symmetry and respond at period 2T. Many-body localization or prethermalization protects this order, which has been seen with trapped ions, NV centres and superconducting qubits.
